label: The Fundamental Group
notes: Open the chapter, which spans printed pages 317 through 371. We enter algebraic topology by associating to a space a group built from loops up to deformation. The fundamental group detects holes, distinguishes spaces, and through covering spaces computes the loops on the circle, yielding striking applications like the fundamental theorem of algebra.

label: Homotopy of Paths
notes: Two paths with the same endpoints are path homotopic when one deforms continuously into the other keeping the endpoints fixed. Path homotopy is an equivalence relation, and concatenation of paths descends to a well-defined operation on classes. These classes are the elements from which the fundamental group is assembled.

label: Definition of the Group
notes: Fixing a base point, the homotopy classes of loops at that point form a group under concatenation, with the constant loop as identity and the reversed loop as inverse. This is the fundamental group. For path connected spaces the choice of base point does not matter up to isomorphism, so it is an invariant of the space.

label: Covering Spaces
notes: A covering space maps onto a base space so that each point has an evenly covered neighborhood, a disjoint union of sheets each mapped homeomorphically. Paths and homotopies lift uniquely once a starting point is chosen. Covering spaces translate questions about the fundamental group into combinatorics of sheets and lifting.

label: The Fundamental Group of the Circle
notes: Using the real line as a covering space of the circle, lifting a loop records how many times it winds around, an integer. This shows the fundamental group of the circle is the integers under addition. It is the first nontrivial computation and the engine behind the chapter's applications.

label: Applications
notes: From the fundamental group of the circle we derive the Brouwer fixed point theorem in two dimensions, the fact that the disk has no retraction onto its boundary, and the fundamental theorem of algebra. These show how an algebraic invariant settles genuinely geometric questions. Next: separation theorems in the plane.
